passage: A leaf blower roars outside the Stockholm flat and Anders, twenty months old, bursts into sobs, arms stiff, face red. His father, Rafael, picks him up and holds him close, swaying. "Loud, loud. I've got you." Anders keeps crying for a long time, far longer than his cousin would. A neighbour in the stairwell frowns. Rafael keeps swaying and humming the same low tune. Slowly the sobs turn to hiccups, and Anders rests his cheek on Rafael's shoulder.

qa.q: What does Rafael say while swaying Anders?
qa.a: "Loud, loud. I've got you."

qa.q: What do Anders's stiff arms and red face suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He is frightened and overwhelmed by the sudden roar.

qa.q: What choice did Rafael make even when the neighbour frowned?
qa.a: He kept swaying and humming the same low tune, offering steady comfort until Anders settled.

qa.q: How might Rafael feel when the neighbour frowns?
qa.a: He may feel judged, as if the crying means bad parenting, but he stays calm and focused on Anders.

grounding: A sensitive toddler cries hard at a loud noise and takes a long time to settle, and his father's steady comfort helps.

passage: I'm Keerthana, a crèche helper. Every morning Uday, two, clings to his mother's dupatta and cries till he's hoarse. When nap time moved, he cried after lunch too; I can't be sure why. His mother once asked me, eyes wet, if she was doing something wrong. I told her no. We keep his blue blanket by the door, sing the same song each morning, and I hold him till he's ready. Last week he pointed at the fish tank sooner.

qa.q: What is kept by the door for Uday?
qa.a: His blue blanket is kept by the door.

qa.q: What might Uday's mother have been feeling when she asked if she was doing something wrong?
qa.a: She seemed worried and guilty, fearing the crying was her fault.

qa.q: What changes did the crèche make to help Uday settle?
qa.a: They kept his blue blanket by the door, sang the same song each morning and held him until he was ready.

qa.q: How does Keerthana see Uday's crying?
qa.a: Keerthana treats it as his sensitivity, not bad behaviour or bad parenting, and answers it with steady comfort.

grounding: A crèche helper describes a toddler who cries hard at separation and changed routines, and reassures his mother it is not her fault.

passage:
Note for Harish's family
Today we had a fire drill. The bell was very loud, and Harish cried hard with his hands over his ears. He was slow to calm. I held him in the quiet corner, rocked slowly and hummed the rain song he likes. He clung to my kurta. Some children bounce back fast; Harish feels things deeply. Before the next drill I'll warn him and cover his ears.
Sunaina, caregiver

qa.q: What song did Sunaina hum?
qa.a: The rain song Harish likes.

qa.q: Why did Harish cry so hard during the drill?
qa.a: The loud bell frightened and overwhelmed him; he feels things deeply and takes a long time to settle.

qa.q: What is Sunaina's plan for the next drill?
qa.a: To warn Harish beforehand and cover his ears, so the bell is less of a shock.

qa.q: How might Harish's family feel reading this note?
qa.a: Reassured that his crying is understood as sensitivity, not bad behaviour, and that he was steadily comforted.

grounding: Shows, in a caregiver's note, a toddler who cries hard at a loud noise and settles slowly, met with steady comfort rather than blame.

passage: When the tractor next door roared to life, Yash screamed and buried his face in Alka's sari. He was still sobbing long after it had rumbled off. His Dadi clicked her tongue. 'You spoil him. Other children don't cry like this.' Alka kept rocking him on the charpai, humming. 'He isn't naughty, Amma. Loud things hit him harder.' Bit by bit his breathing slowed. At last he lifted his head and pointed at the sparrows on the wall.

qa.q: Where did Yash bury his face?
qa.a: In Alka's sari.

qa.q: Why was Yash still sobbing after the tractor had gone?
qa.a: The loud roar frightened him, and he is a sensitive child who takes a long time to settle.

qa.q: What does Alka's response show about comforting a sensitive toddler?
qa.a: Steady rocking and humming, without scolding, helped him calm down bit by bit.

qa.q: How does Dadi see Yash's crying?
qa.a: Dadi thinks Alka spoils him, reading his crying as a sign of poor upbringing rather than sensitivity.

grounding: Shows a toddler who cries hard at a loud noise and settles slowly, and a parent who treats it as sensitivity, not spoiling, and gives steady comfort.

passage: On Monday Tuan's daycare in Melbourne moved him to the bigger room, with a new teacher. When his mum waved goodbye, Tuan howled and clung to the door. He was still crying long after the others had started painting. Rafael, the teacher, sat on the floor near him, holding out Tuan's own blanket from his bag. At last Tuan crawled onto his lap. At pick-up Rafael said, 'Change is hard for him. The same goodbye song every day will help.'

qa.q: What did Rafael hold out to Tuan?
qa.a: Tuan's own blanket from his bag.

qa.q: Why did Tuan cry long after the others started painting?
qa.a: The new room and his mum leaving upset him deeply; a changed routine makes him anxious and slow to settle.

qa.q: Why might the same goodbye song every day help?
qa.a: It adds something predictable to a changed routine, a steady signal that makes goodbyes less frightening.

qa.q: What might Tuan's mum feel as she waves goodbye?
qa.a: She probably felt torn and worried, leaving him howling at the door.

grounding: Shows a toddler deeply upset by separation and a changed routine who settles slowly with steady, patient comfort.

passage:
Monday: The pressure cooker whistled and Anjali screamed and grabbed her mother Manjula's leg. She sobbed long after the kitchen went quiet while Manjula held her and hummed.
Wednesday: Before the whistle, Manjula picked her up. "Loud sound coming." Anjali buried her face and cried a little, then settled sooner in her arms.
Saturday: At the first hiss, Anjali ran to Manjula herself, hands over her ears. Then she peeked out and pointed at the cooker.

qa.q: What made Anjali scream on Monday?
qa.a: The pressure cooker whistled.

qa.q: How was Anjali feeling on Monday, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was frightened and upset: she screamed, grabbed Manjula's leg and sobbed long after the kitchen went quiet.

qa.q: What did Manjula try on Wednesday that helped?
qa.a: She picked Anjali up before the whistle and said, "Loud sound coming," so the noise came with warning and comfort.

qa.q: What is it like for Manjula when Anjali takes so long to settle?
qa.a: It takes patience; Manjula keeps holding and humming instead of scolding, and by Saturday she sees Anjali come to her and even peek at the cooker.

grounding: Shows a toddler who cries hard at a loud noise and settles slowly, and how steady comfort over several days helps.
